text:
## Observations

1. When all in-degrees except those at two vertices are fixed, the feasible in-degrees at either of those two vertices form an integer interval.
2. Every forest omits at least one rim edge, and each resulting rim path can contain at most one vertex whose spoke is selected.
3. Once a rim edge is omitted, a single bit records all the information needed to decide whether another spoke can be selected along the current rim path.

## Solution sketch

> When all in-degrees except those at two vertices are fixed, the feasible in-degrees at either of those two vertices form an integer interval.

1. Use deletion and contraction to show that the number of distinct in-degree sequences equals the number of forests, including the empty forest. To prove the interval property for vertices \(u\) and \(v\), compare two orientations in which \(u\) has lower and higher in-degree. Direct the edges on which they differ as in the lower-in-degree orientation. In this difference graph, \(u\) has excess out-degree, \(v\) has excess in-degree, and every other vertex is balanced. Thus there is a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\). Reversing that path raises the in-degree of \(u\) by one while preserving every in-degree outside \(\{u,v\}\). Repeating gives all intermediate values.

   Now delete a non-loop edge \(uv\) and group the resulting sequences by their in-degrees outside \(\{u,v\}\). Restoring the edge adds exactly one more sequence to each group. If the in-degree interval at \(u\) was \([a,b]\), the two directions together give \([a,b+1]\). The number of groups equals the number of sequences after contracting \(uv\), since the merged in-degree is the sum at \(u\) and \(v\) and is determined by the other in-degrees and the total edge count. This gives the same deletion–contraction recurrence as for forests. Contraction may create parallel edges and loops. Keep parallel edges distinct, and ignore loops in the recurrence since they add a fixed in-degree and cannot belong to a forest. Both counts are one on an edgeless graph, so they agree.

> Every forest omits at least one rim edge, and each resulting rim path can contain at most one vertex whose spoke is selected.

2. Count subsets of edges by scanning the rim in cyclic order. Once at least one rim edge is omitted, the selected rim edges form disjoint paths, including isolated vertices. Two selected spokes on one path would close a cycle through the hub. With at most one selected spoke on each path, the paths can only meet at the hub and no cycle can form. This gives exactly the forest condition.

> Once a rim edge is omitted, a single bit records all the information needed to decide whether another spoke can be selected along the current rim path.

3. At vertex \(i\), use state \(0\) if the current path has no selected spoke yet and state \(1\) if it already has one. First choose whether to select the spoke, which is allowed only in state \(0\) when \(s_i=1\). Then either keep the outgoing rim edge and carry the state forward, or omit it and reset to \(0\). With incoming states as rows and outgoing states as columns, the transition matrix is
   \[
   M_i=\begin{pmatrix}2+s_i&s_i\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Multiply these matrices in input order, starting with the identity, and take the trace of the product to require the state to close around the rim. Any omitted edge forces a reset, so each valid forest determines exactly one closed state sequence. The trace also counts two sequences that keep every rim edge. A closed sequence with no reset must stay in its initial state throughout, giving one sequence for each initial state, both with no selected spokes. Subtract two and print the result modulo \(998244353\).

   With no spokes, this gives \(2^N-1\), the number of proper subsets of the rim edges. With one spoke, it gives \(2(2^N-1)\), since that spoke can be included independently. The same transitions handle adjacent spokes and the case where every spoke is present. Each matrix update takes constant time and can be reduced modulo \(998244353\), for \(O(N)\) total time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the input string.
system_prompt:
You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.
## Solution sketch
Describe one coherent algorithm as numbered steps. Before each step quote the
relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.
Cover edge cases and time/space complexity in the sketch.
Return prose only, without Python implementation or command blocks.
The guide will be implemented by a separate coding agent.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
